title: The Bicycle Makers Who Taught a Machine to Fly
summary: In Dayton, Ohio, Wilbur and Orville Wright spent their working days repairing bicycles.

chapters.title: The Bicycle Makers Who Taught a Machine to Fly

paragraphs.text: In Dayton, Ohio, Wilbur and Orville Wright spent their working days repairing bicycles.
A bicycle had wheels, chains, bearings, and a rider who had to keep it balanced. If a rider leaned carelessly or turned badly, a perfectly good machine could fall over.
That was an important problem to understand for two men who wanted to build an aircraft.

By the end of the nineteenth century, many inventors were trying to fly. Balloons could rise, and gliders could carry people through the air for short distances. But a practical powered aircraft needed to do more than leave the ground.
It had to stay under control.
A machine that lifted a person into the sky but could not turn safely or recover from a tilt was a danger rather than a useful invention.

The Wright brothers studied earlier experiments, including the work of Otto Lilienthal, who had made many gliding flights before dying after a crash in 1896. They corresponded with the experienced aviation experimenter Octave Chanute.
Then they began making their own tests.

For their outdoor work, they chose the coast of North Carolina. Near Kitty Hawk and Kill Devil Hills, wind could provide lift, and broad sandy ground offered a softer place to land than a city street.

Getting there from Ohio required transporting equipment to a remote coast. The brothers worked away from their bicycle shop, living beside the dunes while salt air and blowing sand reached their tools.
Their early gliders had two wings, one above the other.
The wings were curved because their shape helped moving air produce lift. But lift alone did not solve the problem of balance.
An aircraft could tip in three different ways. Its nose could rise or fall. One wing could tilt lower than the other. Its nose could swing to the left or right.
The brothers needed control over all three movements.
They placed a movable surface in front of the wings to control the nose's up-and-down movement. To control the side-to-side tilt, they developed wing warping.
The tips of the wings could be twisted so that the two sides met the air at different angles. One side then produced more lift than the other, helping the pilot correct a tilt.
This made the wings active parts of the steering system.
But the tests did not produce all the results the brothers expected.
In 1901, their glider gave less lift than calculations had suggested. It also behaved badly during some turns. Simply building a larger wing would not explain why the calculations were wrong.
They returned to Dayton and built a wind tunnel.
It was a wooden box with a fan that sent air over small model wings. Inside, measuring devices allowed the brothers to compare different shapes.
The tunnel let them test many designs without building a full aircraft for each one. A wing could be changed, placed in the moving air, and measured against another.

They studied both lift and drag. Lift helped keep an aircraft up. Drag resisted its movement through the air. A wing that produced useful lift while creating too much drag might leave an engine unable to move the aircraft fast enough.
Their measurements gave them better information than the tables they had originally relied on.
In 1902, they returned to North Carolina with a much improved glider.

There was still a steering difficulty. When the wings were warped for a turn, the two sides did not only produce different amounts of lift. They also produced different amounts of drag. That could swing the nose in an unwanted direction.
A movable rear rudder helped control this movement. Used together with wing warping, it allowed the aircraft to turn more effectively.
The brothers made hundreds of gliding flights.
They were learning how to fly before adding an engine.

For the powered machine, they needed an engine light enough to carry but strong enough to drive propellers. Their mechanic, Charlie Taylor, helped build one when available engines did not suit their needs.
The propellers were another engineering problem.
A propeller was not simply a paddle pushing against air. Each blade worked like a wing moving along a turning path. Its shape had to suit the different speeds at different distances from the centre.
The brothers used what they had learned about wings to design efficient wooden propellers. Chains connected the engine to two propellers behind the aircraft.
On 17 December 1903, the machine stood on a launching rail at Kill Devil Hills.
The wind was strong and the weather cold. The pilot would lie on the lower wing rather than sit in an enclosed cabin. There were no comfortable seats, windscreen, or passenger aisle.
Orville made the first flight.
The aircraft left the rail and travelled 120 feet, about 37 metres, in twelve seconds. Its movement was uneven, but it had carried its pilot in powered, controlled flight.
Three more flights followed. The brothers took turns.
On the fourth flight, Wilbur remained in the air for fifty-nine seconds and travelled 852 feet, about 260 metres.
Then a gust overturned the aircraft while it was on the ground. The machine was damaged badly enough to end that day's experiments.
The brothers had flown, but they had not yet built an aircraft ready for ordinary travel.
In the following years, they continued testing near Dayton. They improved the controls, made longer flights, and developed a machine that could turn, circle, and return to its starting area.
The short journeys over the sand were the beginning of a much larger change. Powered flight would alter transport, exploration, communication, and warfare.
The 1903 aircraft is preserved in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. Its cloth-covered wings and exposed framework look fragile beside modern airliners.
Yet the central problems are recognisable.
An aircraft still needs lift. It still needs power. And it still needs a way to control every movement through the air.
The bicycle makers succeeded by working through those problems separately, then fitting their answers into one machine.
